endorsements.title: Personal Care Utility: Health as Everyday Infrastructure

endorsements.quote: Instead, they are intended to serve surgeons, dermatologists, and mental health professionals as early alert systems, particularly during pre-procedure digital intake or first consultations, to prompt more thorough psychological assessment when needed.

endorsements.title: Ethical Risks and Structural Implications of AI-Mediated Medical Interpreting

endorsements.quote: Statement 4. CADx can be used for characterization of polyps but is not yet ready to determine the necessity of polypectomy.

endorsements.title: Consensus statement on the application of artificial intelligence in osteoporosis screening and management: perspectives from the Asia-Pacific region
endorsements.issuer: Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA

endorsements.title: Digital Twins as catalysts for Whole Person Health Mind Body Medicine in Integrative Oncology
endorsements.quote: Accordingly, Digital Twins should support self-care, symptom management, prevention, and survivorship while keeping diagnosis, prognosis, and cancer treatment decisions within health professionals oversight.

endorsements.title: Digital infrastructures and data interoperability in radiology for prevention: from digital health to AI-enabled, quantitative imaging workflows

endorsements.quote: In tumor staging, AI can serve as an assistive tool but should not replace comprehensive clinical judgment in the absence of sufficient prospective evidence.

endorsements.quote: Users should ensure that LLM outputs are responsibly used as support tools, not as independent replacements for the judgment of healthcare practitioners.

endorsements.title: Operationalizing AI-Enabled Cardiovascular Biomarkers: A Clinician-Centered Framework for Validation, Governance, and Workflow Integration
endorsements.quote: Its intended use must remain narrow: the output is a screening prompt for confirmatory assessment, not a diagnosis of heart failure or an independent indication for treatment.

endorsements.title: Validation and reporting standards for dental artificial intelligence: Lessons from materials biosafety
endorsements.quote: That is the same “assistant, not replacement” position the orthodontic community has reached elsewhere – sound as a principle, but not yet operationalized as an evidentiary requirement.

evidence.title: AI-Human Hybrid Workflow Enhances Teleophthalmology for the Detection of Diabetic Retinopathy
evidence.outcome: specificity and sensitivity for DR
evidence.effect: A hybrid AI-human workflow achieved 95.5% sensitivity and 98.2% specificity, compared to 60.3% specificity for AI alone.
evidence.quote: A 2-step AI-human hybrid workflow in which the AI algorithm initially rendered an assessment followed by overread by a retina specialist of MTMDR-positive encounters resulted in a sensitivity of 95.5% (95% CI, 86.7%-100%) and a specificity of 98.2% (95% CI, 94.6%-100%).

evidence.title: Impact of real-life use of artificial intelligence as support for human reading in a population-based breast cancer screening program with mammography and tomosynthesis
evidence.outcome: Cancer detection, recall rate, PPV with AI as concurrent reading support vs without
evidence.effect: CDR 9.0‰ vs 5.8‰ (+3.2‰, p<0.001); PPV 14.6% vs 10.6% (+4%, p<0.001); recall rate 6.1% vs 5.4% (+0.7%, p<0.001); radiologists made final recall decision.
evidence.quote: The implementation of an AI system for concurrent decision support for reading DM and DBT screening exams increased the breast cancer detection rate (CDR) by 3.2‰ (9.0‰ vs 5.8‰; p < 0.001) and the positive predictive value (PPV) of the recalled women by 4% (14.6% vs 10.6%; p < 0.001) with an acceptable increase in recall rate (RR) by 0.7% (6.1% vs 5.4%; p < 0.001).
evidence.sample_unit: women (screening examinations; 11,998 AI-supported and 11,998 matched historical controls)

evidence.title: Diagnostic performance with and without artificial intelligence assistance in real-world screening mammography
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic performance of radiologists using AI assistance versus stand-alone AI
evidence.effect: Radiologists with AI-CAD versus stand-alone AI-CAD: sensitivity 76.5% in both; specificity 92.3% vs 93.8%; AUC 0.844 vs 0.851; recall rates 8.8% vs. 7.4%; no statistically significant differences.
evidence.quote: Radiologists with AI-CAD assistance showed the same sensitivity (76.5%) and similar specificity (92.3% vs 93.8%), AUC (0.844 vs 0.851), and recall rates (8.8% vs. 7.4%) compared to standalone AI-CAD.

evidence.title: Standalone AI Versus AI-Assisted Radiologists in Emergency ICH Detection: A Prospective, Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of standalone AI vs AI-assisted radiologists for ICH
evidence.effect: Radiologists with AI outperformed standalone AI: sensitivity 98.91% vs 95.91%, specificity 99.83% vs 87.35%, accuracy 99.53% vs 90.11% (p<0.001); false positives 293 vs 4.
evidence.quote: Radiologists demonstrated statistically significant superiority across all main diagnostic metrics.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence-based smartphone application for skin cancer detection: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of CNN alone vs CNN plus teledermatology review
evidence.effect: CNN alone: sensitivity 82.5%, specificity 76.8%. With teledermatology review: specificity rose to 86.8% (P < 0.001) but sensitivity fell to 75.3%.
evidence.quote: Combined CNN and teledermatology review resulted in increased specificity (86.8%; P < 0.001), with a sensitivity of 75.3%.

evidence.title: Prospective multi-centre evaluation of guideline-based artificial intelligence to streamline multidisciplinary tumour board
evidence.outcome: Change in diagnosis and treatment plan at 1 and 6 months
evidence.effect: Change D+TP at 6 months: MTB only 28.08%, AI only 24.3%, MTB+AI 14.73%. At 1 month: 13.12%, 8.78%, 4.86%. MTB+AI significantly lower than both. Groups were not randomized.
evidence.quote: The combination of the MTB with AI gives the most effective result in reducing the change in D and TP from 28.08% to 14.73% within 6 months (13.12% vs 4.86% in 1 month).

evidence.title: AI-assisted vs. textbook-based vs. blended learning for acute abdomen diagnosis: a retrospective cohort study of emergency interns
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy using AI combined with traditional resources vs primarily AI
evidence.effect: Accuracy 87.1% blended vs 82.4% AI-assisted; difference not significant (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.41–1.16, p=0.209). Missed diagnoses 6.7% blended vs 14.3% AI-assisted; misdiagnosis 6.2% vs 3.3%.
evidence.quote: The difference between AI-assisted and blended learning was not statistically significant (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.41–1.16, p = 0.209).

evidence.title: The Impact of a Neuroradiologist on the Report of a Real-World CT Perfusion Imaging Map Derived from Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning-Driven Software
evidence.outcome: proportion of reportable CTP cases
evidence.effect: AI-derived CTP maps were reportable in 65.2% of cases without artifacts and improved to 87.9% when reviewed by neuroradiologists.
evidence.quote: The study found that CTP maps derived from AI software were reportable in 65.2% of cases without artifacts and improved to 87.9% reportable cases when reviewed by neuroradiologists.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in emergency skeletal X-ray: post-deployment monitoring and clinical impact of incorrect AI results
evidence.outcome: patient pathway alterations
evidence.effect: Radiographer supervision altered the patient pathway in 20% of cases compared to AI alone, frequently overriding incorrect AI results.
evidence.quote: Compared to AI's initial suggestion, radiographer supervision altered the subsequent patient pathway in 20% of the cases, with the likelihood overriding AI being higher when AI results were later found to be incorrect (i.e. false positives or false negatives).

evidence.title: Methylation profiling in CNS tumor diagnostics: a single-centre real-world experience from Central Europe
evidence.venue: Virchows Archiv : an international journal of pathology
evidence.outcome: Clinical usefulness of classifier output when integrated with histomorphology and ancillary markers
evidence.effect: 52.7% of lower-confidence cases yielded meaningful clinical integration when supported by histomorphology and ancillary markers; discrepant or misleading classifications occurred in 1.9%.
evidence.quote: Crucially, over half (52.7%) of the lower-confidence cases yielded meaningful clinical integration when supported by histomorphology and ancillary genetic or immunohistochemical markers, demonstrating that rigid score cutoffs should not dictate assay failure.

evidence.title: Grounding Large Language Model in Clinical Diagnostics
evidence.outcome: diagnostic accuracy and efficiency
evidence.effect: Collaboration between ClinDiag-GPT and physicians enhanced both diagnostic accuracy and efficiency compared to ClinDiag-GPT alone and physicians alone.
evidence.quote: Collaboration between ClinDiag-GPT and physicians enhanced both diagnostic accuracy and efficiency, demonstrating ClinDiag-GPT's potential as a valuable clinical assistant.

evidence.title: Optical Biopsy of Dysplasia in Barrett's Oesophagus Assisted by Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Dysplasia detection sensitivity of AI-assisted gastroenterologists versus standalone AI
evidence.effect: AI-assisted gastroenterologists outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% [95% CI 2.11–23.67], p = 0.024).
evidence.quote: Additionally, they outperformed the sensitivity of the AI model alone (+12.89% (2.11–23.67), p = 0.024) ( Figure 4 D).

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.outcome: standalone AI versus standard care
evidence.effect: AI standalone sensitivity was lower than standard care, 75.0% vs 79.8%; specificity was non-inferior, 96.0% vs 96.0%.
evidence.quote: However, operating as a sole reader, the AI reader had lower sensitivity (75.0 vs. 79.8%; P < 1.98 × 10 −5 ) at non-inferior specificity (96.0 vs. 96.0%: P = 0.56) than the current standard of care (two readers with arbitration; Supplementary Tables 1 , 2 ).

evidence.title: Grading of diabetic retinopathy using a pre-segmenting deep learning classification model: Validation of an automated algorithm
evidence.outcome: diabetic retinopathy classification sensitivity and specificity
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 95%, 94%, and 78% for human grader alone, human grader with AI assistance, and autonomous AI, respectively; specificities were 83%, 84%, and 81%.
evidence.quote: The sensitivity for Models 1–3 was 95%, 94% and 78%, and specificities were 83%, 84% and 81% (Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Deep Learning Algorithms for Breast Cancer Detection in a UK Screening Cohort: As Stand-alone Readers and Combined with Human Readers
evidence.outcome: combined human-AI screening accuracy
evidence.effect: DL+human sensitivity 67.0%, 65.6%, 65.4% vs double reading 67.4%; specificity 97.4%, 97.6%, 97.6% vs 97.1%; P<.001 for all.
evidence.quote: Combining the DL algorithms with human readers achieved noninferior sensitivity (67.0%, 65.6%, and 65.4% for DL-1, DL-2, and DL-3, respectively; P < .001 for all) compared with double reading (67.4%), and superior specificity (97.4%, 97.6%, and 97.6%; P < .001 for all) compared with double reading (97.1%).

evidence.title: Clinician-artificial intelligence collaboration: A win-win solution for efficiency and reliability in atrial fibrillation diagnosis
evidence.outcome: PAF diagnostic correctness
evidence.effect: All patients were correctly identified, and clinicians' workload was reduced by 76.7%.
evidence.quote: After implementing the proposed clinician-AI collaboration strategy, all patients were correctly identified, and clinicians' workload was reduced by 76.7%.

evidence.title: AI for fracture diagnosis in clinical practice: Four approaches to systematic AI-implementation and their impact on AI-effectiveness
evidence.outcome: standalone versus adjunct fracture diagnosis errors
evidence.effect: Safety-net had 0.07% FN (1/1508; 1 consequence) versus standalone 1.5% FN (23/1508; 11 consequences), but FP was 7.6% versus 6.8%.
evidence.quote: Best results were obtained implementing AI as safety net, which eliminates missed fractures with serious clinical consequences; even though false positives are increased, unnecessary treatments are limited.

evidence.title: Multimodal Generative Artificial Intelligence Model for Creating Radiology Reports for Chest Radiographs in Patients Undergoing Tuberculosis Screening
evidence.outcome: standalone versus adjunct diagnosis
evidence.effect: AI report accuracy was 90.8%; reader-with-AI accuracies were 94.1% and 93.5%.
evidence.quote: For detection of tuberculosis-related abnormalities, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 95.2%, 86.7%, and 90.8% for AI-generated reports; 93.1%, 93.6%, and 93.4% for reader 1 without AI-generated reports; 93.1%, 95.0%, and 94.1% for reader 1 with AI-generated reports; 95.8%, 87.2%, and 91.3% for reader 2 without AI-generated reports; and 95.8%, 91.5%, and 93.5% for reader 2 with AI-generated reports.
evidence.country: Unknown (public datasets from tuberculosis screening programs)

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Performance of LLM-Assisted Arterial Blood Gas Interpretation: A Single-Center Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: agreement on primary and secondary acid-base disorders
evidence.effect: APSD agreement was moderate for standalone LLM-I (ChatGPT κ=0.65, Copilot κ=0.61, Gemini κ=0.62) but strong for supervised LLM-S (ChatGPT κ=0.91, Copilot κ=0.81, Gemini κ=0.81).
evidence.quote: For identifying both primary and secondary disorders regardless of order (APSD), LLM-I showed moderate agreement (ChatGPT κ = 0.65, Copilot κ = 0.61, Gemini κ = 0.62), whereas LLM-S achieved strong agreement (ChatGPT κ = 0.91, Copilot κ = 0.81, Gemini κ = 0.81).

evidence.title: AI-Powered Chest X-Ray for Diagnosing Pulmonary Tuberculosis in County and Township Health Care Facilities in Yichang: Retrospective, Real-World Study
evidence.outcome: CAD triage workload and yield
evidence.effect: Selective review reduced radiologist workload 85.5%, with minimum DYD 25.6% and potential DYD 83.9%.
evidence.quote: Strategy 5 enabled a radiologist workload reduction of 85.5% (1‐13,515/93,319) while maintaining a minimum system DYD of 25.6% (ie, finding all cases the radiologists originally found) and a potential DYD of 83.9% (if radiologists trusted the AI on all 229 positive cases; Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.outcome: CIN2+ agreement under human-in-the-loop review versus standalone AI
evidence.effect: Agreement with P2-digital increased from 88.7% (kappa 0.74) for EagleEye alone to 90.7% (kappa 0.79) for AI-assisted review (EE + P2).
evidence.quote: Relative to P2-digital, agreement with the algorithm increased from 88.7% (κ = 0.74) for EE alone to 90.7% (κ = 0.79) for EE + P2, indicating incremental value of human adjudication in a human-in-the-loop workflow, where the expert accepts or dismisses AI-suggested foci.

evidence.title: Diagnosing growth in low-grade gliomas with and without artificial intelligence-measured longitudinal volume measurements: A retrospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of AI-only versus AI with physician oversight for detecting tumor growth
evidence.effect: AI alone yielded 25% false positive and 8.33% false negative rates, including 3/7 negative controls wrongly flagged; with physician review all 7 controls were correctly stable.
evidence.quote: In contrast, without human oversight, 3 out of 7 cases were incorrectly flagged as tumor growth.

evidence.title: External validation of a commercial AI system for pulmonary embolism detection on chest CTPA: a multicenter study
evidence.outcome: Adjunct (radiologist plus AI) versus AI standalone diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: AI alone had 43 errors (36 false positives); radiologist plus AI had 7 errors and higher AUC 0.928-0.934 than AI alone 0.807-0.810.
evidence.quote: The superior performance of the combined approach suggests that AI systems function most effectively as assistive tools rather than replacement technologies, augmenting human expertise rather than superseding it.

evidence.title: Combining Machine Learning Models and Screening to Enhance Suicide Risk Identification for American Indian Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of ML plus screening in parallel (ML as adjunct) versus screening alone
evidence.effect: Parallel ASQ or ML medium/high risk sensitivity 0.795 (95% CI 0.671-0.920) vs ASQ alone 0.178, without missing any cases caught by screening; PPV 0.012.
evidence.quote: Instead, parallel testing brings immediate value to the field by preserving universal screening and allowing ML to act as a clinical “safety net” to identify at-risk patients who are missed by current practices.

evidence.title: Human-in-the-Loop Enhances Machine Learning Inference in Intraoperative Optical Coherence Tomography Glioma Imaging
evidence.outcome: HITL adjunct versus standalone model diagnosis
evidence.effect: HITL sensitivity 98% [92–100] versus Gemini 86% [74–95].
evidence.quote: When compared to the advanced Gemini 3.1 Pro baseline, the human inference on Segmentation maps maintained a pronounced and significant edge in sensitivity (98% [92–100] vs. 86% [74–95]).
evidence.sample_unit: intraoperative OCT scans (27 patients; 5 neurosurgeon raters)

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Infectious Disease Decision-Making: From Examination to Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: completeness of clinical case decision-making
evidence.effect: Doctors supported by LLMs achieved significantly higher completeness scores compared with both doctors alone (p = 0.0015) and LLMs alone (p = 0.0010).
evidence.quote: Post hoc analysis demonstrated that doctors supported by LLMs achieved significantly higher completeness scores compared with both the doctors alone ( p = 0.0015) and the LLMs alone ( p = 0.0010).

evidence.title: Performance of the Techcyte AI-based image analysis system for coproparasitological diagnosis in clinical stool specimens: a retrospective evaluation study
evidence.outcome: AI-only versus AI plus operator review agreement with microscopy, negative specimen handling
evidence.effect: AI alone correctly identified 2/31 (6.45%) negatives; after operator review 29/29 (100%) concordance; overall PPA 96.62%, NPA 93.33% with review.
evidence.quote: Before operator review, most of negative specimens 29/31 (93.54%) were considered positive by the AI-based software due to artifact misclassification.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in population breast cancer screening: A two-year cost-effectiveness analysis
evidence.outcome: cancer detection with AI-only low-risk triage
evidence.effect: Triage Only saved $4/person but detected 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 vs standard; ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected.
evidence.quote: In the base-case analysis, Triage Only was the most efficient strategy, saving an average of $4 per person screened but detecting 0.521 fewer cancers per 1000 people screened compared to standard practice (ICER $8206 per additional cancer detected).

evidence.title: Evaluating Artificial Intelligence as a First-Pass Reader in Fundus Photograph Screening: A Multireader Workflow Validation Study
evidence.outcome: AI-human double-reading performance
evidence.effect: Human reads 1.02–1.11 vs 2.00–2.10; DR/RVO no significant loss; AMD sensitivity 0.842–0.950 vs 0.845, specificity ≥0.978.
evidence.quote: AI–human double reading with arbitration substantially reduced repeated human reading while preserving diagnostic reliability for DR and RVO and demonstrating reader-configuration-dependent performance for AMD.

evidence.title: Evaluating an AI-assisted triage workflow for retinal diseases
evidence.outcome: Missed disease when AI-negative outputs substituted for diagnosis
evidence.effect: DR sensitivity decreased 0.9168 to 0.8838 (difference -0.0330; p < 0.001); AMD 0.8570 to 0.8445 (difference -0.0124; p = 0.008).
evidence.quote: AI-assisted negative-screening can reduce ophthalmologist workload across multiple retinal diseases, but with disease-specific safety trade-offs: because AI-negative images are not reviewed, reduced sensitivity for DR and AMD means a small proportion of true-positive cases would go undetected, potentially delaying diagnosis and treatment for sight-threatening disease.

evidence.title: AI-assisted cardiomegaly screening via implicit morphological inference and human-in-the-loop validation
evidence.venue: Journal of X-ray science and technology
evidence.outcome: cardiomegaly screening accuracy
evidence.effect: expert-guided refinement improved accuracy from 90.31% to 93.63% on NIH and from 76.07% to 91.21% on OpenI (p<0.001)
evidence.quote: Crucially, the integration of a Human-in-the-Loop mechanism successfully neutralized domain shifts; the McNemar test confirmed that expert-guided refinement provided statistically significant accuracy improvements to 93.63% and 91.21% on NIH and OpenI, respectively (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of Brainomix e-Stroke software
evidence.outcome: Accuracy limits of AI imaging output relevant to use as stand-alone diagnosis
evidence.effect: Hyperdense thrombus PPV was 22.9% with many false positives; e-ASPECTS sensitivity 58.6%; authors conclude it should be an adjunct to expert interpretation, not standalone.
evidence.quote: The accuracy for identifying hyperdense thrombus was lower (69.1%), which was mainly due to many false positives (positive predictive value of 22.9%).

evidence.title: Towards clinical implementation of an AI-algorithm for detection of cervical spine fractures on computed tomography
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of AI versus radiology reference standard
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 89.8%, specificity 95.3%, PPV 63.0%; clinically relevant fractures missed despite high accuracy.
evidence.quote: Although AI-assisted workflow prioritization of cervical spine fractures on CT shows high diagnostic accuracy, clinically relevant cases were missed.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence software for assessing brain ischemic penumbra/core infarction on computed tomography perfusion: A real-world accuracy study
evidence.outcome: AI CT perfusion penumbra/core assessment inaccuracy versus expert consensus
evidence.effect: AI perfusion diagnosis judged invalid in 3 of 22 patients (inaccuracy rate 13.6%); authors conclude integrating CT, CTA, and MRI data is crucial for MT decisions.
evidence.quote: The computed tomography (CT) perfusion diagnosis by Shukun (AI) was confirmed to be invalid in 3 patients (inaccuracy rate: 13.6%).

evidence.title: Prospective Diagnostic Accuracy and Technical Feasibility of Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Rib Fracture Detection on Chest Radiographs: Observational Study
evidence.outcome: Error rates of AI rib fracture detection relevant to stand-alone diagnostic use
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 74.5%, PPV 24.2%; false-positive and false-negative rates indicate AI should be a supportive screening tool, not stand-alone diagnostic.
evidence.quote: Although the system showed high negative predictive value, the observed false-positive and false-negative rates indicate that it should be considered a supportive screening tool rather than a stand-alone diagnostic solution or a replacement for clinical judgment.

evidence.title: Real-world diagnostic performance of artificial intelligence in skin cancer screening
evidence.outcome: AI diagnostic accuracy of exact diagnosis and lesion type versus dermatologists
evidence.effect: AI correct precise diagnosis 28.6% vs dermatologists 61.6% (P<0.001); correct tumour/lesion type 51.4% vs 75.5% (P<0.001); PPV 46.5% vs 62.1%.
evidence.quote: AI correctly identified the precise diagnosis 28.6% of the time, compared with dermatologists 61.6% of the time (P < 0.001).

evidence.title: Evaluating the usability and practicality of AI-enabled smartphone-based obstetric ultrasound in Sierra Leone: a mixed-methods study
evidence.outcome: Substitution of ultrasound for essential antenatal clinical assessments
evidence.effect: Some providers substituted ultrasound for physical examinations and vital sign checks. Findings were qualitative; resulting diagnostic errors or patient harms were not quantified.
evidence.quote: Although the device was widely accepted, the study revealed over-reliance on the device, with some providers substituting essential clinical practices like physical examinations and vital sign checks.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-Based CTA Software for Real-World Detection of Large-Vessel Occlusion in Acute Ischemic Stroke
evidence.outcome: AI sensitivity for occlusions by location, supporting adjunct rather than standalone use
evidence.effect: Lower sensitivity for distal M1 (73%, κ = 0.48) and nontarget occlusions excluded; authors conclude e-CTA should be adjunctive, not standalone.
evidence.quote: However, lower sensitivity for intermediate and distal M1 occlusions and the exclusion of nontarget occlusions from the primary endpoint indicate that e-CTA should be used as an adjunctive workflow tool rather than as a standalone method for treatment decision-making.

evidence.title: Accuracy of AI-Driven Cephalometric Tracing Systems in Orthodontic Analysis Including Patients With Cleft Lip/Palate
evidence.outcome: Reliability of AI cephalometric tracing for clinical use without human oversight
evidence.effect: High concordance with computer-assisted manual tracing overall, but not sufficiently reliable in clinical practice without human oversight; Mthd significantly affected 62 of 85 measurements.
evidence.quote: Conclusion Although cephalometric landmark detection and measurements from AudaxCeph, OrthoDx, and WebCeph show high concordance with computer-assisted manual tracing, their use in clinical practice is not sufficiently reliable without human oversight.

evidence.title: AI Decision Support for Challenging Teledermatology Cases: MedGemma Performance in the Dermatology ECHO Program
evidence.outcome: Top-1 and top-k diagnostic accuracy of AI on challenging teledermatology cases
evidence.effect: Strict top-1 accuracy 0.0% (0/77), 3.9% at top-10; relaxed concept-level top-1 28.6%, top-10 45.5%, so the model is unreliable as a stand-alone diagnosis.
evidence.quote: MedGemma achieved 0.0% strict top-1 accuracy, 1.3% top-3 accuracy, 3.9% top-5 accuracy, and 3.9% top-10 accuracy.

evidence.title: Multicentre external validation of a commercial artificial intelligence software to analyse chest radiographs in health screening environments with low disease prevalence
evidence.outcome: Standalone AI lesion detection
evidence.effect: AI detected 12 of 41 pneumonia, 3 of 5 tuberculosis, and 9 of 22 tumours; overall sensitivity was 35.3%.
evidence.quote: AI detected 12 of 41 pneumonia, 3 of 5 tuberculosis, and 9 of 22 tumours.

evidence.title: Population-wide evaluation of artificial intelligence and radiologist assessment of screening mammograms
evidence.outcome: Screen-detected and interval cancer detection
evidence.effect: AI_sens/AI_spec detected fewer screen-detected cancers (1166/1156 vs 1252) but more interval cancers (126/117 vs 39), p<0.0001.
evidence.quote: Both AI<sub>sens</sub> and AI<sub>spec</sub> detected significantly fewer screen-detected cancers (1166 (AI<sub>sens</sub>), 1156 (AI<sub>spec</sub>) vs 1252; p < 0.0001) but found more interval cancers compared to first readers (126 (AI<sub>sens</sub>), 117 (AI<sub>spec</sub>) vs 39; p < 0.0001) with varying types of cancers detected across multiple subgroups.

evidence.title: Potential impact of a new sepsis prediction model for the primary care setting: early health economic evaluation using an observational cohort
evidence.outcome: Adequacy of model score as replacement for clinical judgement
evidence.effect: Authors conclude discrimination is insufficient to replace GP judgement; advise using score to estimate risk within overall judgement rather than strict cut-offs.
evidence.quote: Given the results of the current study, it can be concluded that the discrimination of our new sepsis score is not sufficient to replace the clinical judgement of the GP based on the results of this early economic evaluation.

evidence.title: Doctor's Orders-Why Radiologists Should Consider Adjusting Commercial Machine Learning Applications in Chest Radiography to Fit Their Specific Needs
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of combined comprehensive reading of seven abnormalities without human supervision
evidence.effect: Combined reading: sensitivity 31.37%, specificity 14.55%; 364 (76.31%) patients with false positives and 35 (7.34%) with missed findings; not suitable for unsupervised use.
evidence.quote: Therefore and as of today, DL applications appear not to be suitable for completely unsupervised application in the clinical setting.

evidence.title: Assessing GPT-4 multimodal performance in radiological image analysis
evidence.outcome: Reliability of GPT-4V as standalone diagnostic tool; diagnostic hallucination rate
evidence.effect: Pathology identification only 35.2% correct; authors report diagnostic hallucination rate >40% and state it cannot be trusted as a standalone clinical tool.
evidence.quote: Although GPT-4V shows promise in radiological image interpretation, its high diagnostic hallucination rate (> 40%) indicates it cannot be trusted for clinical use as a standalone tool.
evidence.sample_unit: emergency room diagnostic images (US, CT, X-ray)

evidence.title: Comparison of AI-integrated pathways with human-AI interaction in population mammographic screening for breast cancer
evidence.outcome: cancer detection sensitivity of standalone AI versus standard of care
evidence.effect: Operating as a sole reader, AI had significantly lower sensitivity (75.0% vs 79.8%, P < 1.98 x 10^-5) at non-inferior specificity (96.0% vs 96.0%, P = 0.56) than standard of care.
evidence.quote: However, operating as a sole reader, the AI reader had lower sensitivity (75.0 vs. 79.8%; P < 1.98 × 10 −5 ) at non-inferior specificity (96.0 vs. 96.0%: P = 0.56) than the current standard of care (two readers with arbitration; Supplementary Tables 1 , 2 ).

evidence.title: Revolution or risk?-Assessing the potential and challenges of GPT-4V in radiologic image interpretation
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of autonomous GPT-4V radiologic image interpretation
evidence.effect: Accuracy was 8.3% uncontextualized, 29.1% contextualized first diagnosis, and 63.6% with correct diagnosis among differentials.
evidence.quote: With its pronounced propensity to favor context over image information, the tool's diagnostic accuracy improved from 8.3% (uncontextualized) to 29.1% (contextualized, first diagnosis correct) and 63.6% (contextualized, correct diagnosis among differential diagnoses) (p ≤ 0.001, Cochran's Q test).

evidence.title: Evaluating ChatGPT for neurocognitive disorder diagnosis: a multicenter study
evidence.outcome: Agreement between ChatGPT diagnoses and clinician diagnoses of neurocognitive disorders
evidence.effect: Study 1: fair agreement with clinicians (kappa = .33, chi-square(9) = 6021.96, p < .001); Study 2: no significant diagnostic agreement between ChatGPT versions and clinicians.
evidence.quote: Although ChatGPT 4 Omni shows potential in aligning with clinician diagnoses, its diagnostic accuracy is insufficient for clinical application without human oversight.
evidence.sample_unit: older adults (NACC Uniform Data Set 3 records; Study 1)

evidence.title: Decoding wisdom: Evaluating ChatGPT's accuracy and reproducibility in analyzing orthopantomographic images for third molar assessment
evidence.outcome: Accuracy of ChatGPT-4o interpretation of orthopantomograms for third molar assessment
evidence.effect: Accuracy was 38.44% (95% CI 35.27%-41.62%); responses frequently incomplete or fabricated, insufficient for unsupervised clinical use.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-4o achieved an accuracy rate of 38.44 % (95 % CI: 35.27 %-41.62 %).
evidence.sample_unit: ChatGPT-4o responses (30 per each of 30 orthopantomograms)

evidence.title: Optimizing Artificial Intelligence Thresholds for Mammographic Lesion Detection: A Retrospective Study on Diagnostic Performance and Radiologist-Artificial Intelligence Discordance
evidence.outcome: AI score discrimination in BI-RADS 4A and discordant cases, supporting decision-support use only
evidence.effect: AUC 0.685 for 4A; in 4B/4C lesions with AI scores <35, 19.5% were malignant with no significant AI score difference between benign and malignant, so AI cannot be relied on alone.
evidence.quote: the thresholds should be applied with caution, as current AI systems may not be reliable enough for independent decision-making in the absence of radiologist input.

evidence.title: Human-AI collectives most accurately diagnose clinical vignettes
evidence.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic miss rates of stand-alone LLMs compared with physician diagnoses
evidence.effect: LLMs missed correct diagnosis in 34% to 54% of cases; individual physicians correctly identified the diagnosis in 30% to 38% of those cases (ranking it first in 20% to 26%).
evidence.quote: Crucially, when LLMs did not list the correct diagnosis at all (range across LLMs: 34% to 54%; Right -most columns), individual humans did mention it in a substantial number of cases (range across LLMs: 30% to 38%; Right -most columns excluding Bottom - Right cells), most frequently ranking it first (range across LLMs: 20% to 26%, Top - Right cells).
evidence.sample_unit: text-based medical case vignettes (40,762 physician differential diagnoses)

evidence.title: Dual site external validation of artificial intelligence-enabled treatment monitoring for neovascular age-related macular degeneration in England
evidence.outcome: Errors of autonomous AI assessment and complementarity with clinician errors
evidence.effect: R9 gave 15 false negatives and 84 false positives; 57 errors not made in real-world care, with non-anatomical segmentations in poor-quality images, suggesting clinician-AI interaction could mitigate risks.
evidence.quote: AI-led assessments of nAMD disease activity and those made in real-world care commonly disagreed with the reference standard for different clinical cases.

evidence.title: Deep learning based semi-automated model can predict lineage in patients with pituitary neuroendocrine tumors
evidence.outcome: diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Using the fully automated model as a stand-alone diagnostic resulted in a 5.9% decrease in accuracy compared to standard-of-care manual review.
evidence.quote: However, it demonstrated a 5.9% decrease in accuracy and a 0.011 reduction in the AUC ( p < 0.001), compared to diagnoses based on IHC and manual review (Fig. 2 ).

evidence.title: Comparative Evaluation and Performance of Large Language Models in Clinical Infection Control Scenarios: A Benchmark Study
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LLM outputs for autonomous use versus adjunct use in infection control
evidence.effect: Critical errors found in all models; authors conclude LLMs are not reliable for autonomous use and should serve as adjuncts.
evidence.quote: While GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek V3 deliver useful IPC advice, they are not yet reliable for autonomous use.
evidence.sample_unit: clinical infection control scenarios (165 outputs rated by 16 experts)

evidence.title: Evaluation of the effectiveness of the ChatGPT artificial intelligence application in the diagnosis of spontaneous pneumothorax on chest radiograph interpretation
evidence.outcome: ChatGPT sensitivity for pneumothorax on chest radiographs, by size
evidence.effect: Overall sensitivity 70.9%, NPV 76.8%; AUC 0.894 for large vs 0.439 for small pneumothoraces, so missed diagnoses likely if used standalone.
evidence.quote: However, its limited sensitivity for small pneumothoraces raises significant concerns about its reliability in clinical decision-making.

evidence.title: Evaluating the clinical utility of multimodal large language models in rare maculopathy
evidence.outcome: stand-alone diagnostic performance
evidence.effect: Best all-modality MLLM accuracy was 0.351 with broad choices and 0.561 with limited choices plus demographics.
evidence.quote: However, currently, in rare diseases such as the maculopathies studied in the present paper, MLLMs perform poorly when compared to retinal specialists, and their use is unlikely to aid clinical assessment.

evidence.title: Implementation of a net benefit parameter in ROC curve decision thresholds for AI-powered mammography screening
evidence.outcome: Standalone AI classifications versus radiologist reference
evidence.effect: For both Youden and NB thresholds, all McNemar comparisons to ground truth were <0.0001; authors reported classification errors persisted.
evidence.quote: The AI results differed significantly from the radiologist interpretations, regardless of the threshold determination method, while still exhibiting classification errors.

evidence.title: Performance of ChatGPT-5 in Diagnosing Fractures on Proximal Humerus and Intertrochanteric Femur X-Rays
evidence.outcome: Fracture detection specificity of ChatGPT-5 on hip radiographs (false positives) as standalone diagnostic
evidence.effect: IT femur: 100% sensitivity but only 16.7% specificity (κ = 0.24); hallucinated fractures in normal hip X-rays; proximal humerus 87.5% sensitivity, 100% specificity (κ = 0.74).
evidence.quote: However, limitations in specificity and fine-detail recognition restrict its autonomous clinical use.

evidence.title: Diagnostic Performance of ChatGPT-5 for Detecting Pediatric Pneumothorax on Chest Radiographs: A Multi-Prompt Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity for pediatric pneumothorax, especially small pneumothoraces
evidence.effect: Sensitivity 0.57-0.61 overall; small pneumothoraces ACCP 0.18-0.22 and BTS 0.41-0.46 versus large ACCP 0.75-0.79 and BTS 0.85-0.88.
evidence.quote: However, sensitivity was limited (0.57-0.61) and substantially lower for small pneumothoraces (American College of Chest Physicians [ACCP]: 0.18-0.22; British Thoracic Society [BTS]: 0.41-0.46) than for large pneumothoraces (ACCP: 0.75-0.79; BTS: 0.85-0.88).

evidence.title: Evaluation of multimodal large language models for pneumothorax assessment in real-world clinical scenarios
evidence.outcome: Reliability of multimodal LLM diagnostic output, motivating adjunct rather than stand-alone use
evidence.effect: Limitations in localisation (sensitivity 10-14%), type determination, and management decisions (tube thoracostomy sensitivity 46.2-57.7%) restrict use to cautious supportive roles.
evidence.quote: Multimodal LLMs demonstrated high sensitivity in ruling out pneumothorax; however, limitations in agreement, localisation, and management decisions restrict their role to cautious, supportive use under specialist supervision.

evidence.title: Bot vs. doc-who is better at reading proximal humerus fracture x-rays?
evidence.outcome: Incorrect or missed diagnoses when general-purpose AI interprets radiographs
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-5 missed 23.5% of isolated PHFx x-rays as normal; inter-rater reliability with the attending was slight to poor for fracture characterization.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT incorrectly diagnosed 23.5% of isolated PHFx x-rays as normal, 8.8% with an isolated glenohumeral dislocation without fracture, and 5.7% with a PHFx dislocation.
evidence.sample_unit: shoulder x-rays (35 proximal humerus fracture, 35 normal)

evidence.title: Real-world evaluation of large language models in detecting drug-related problems: A clinical pharmacist-AI concordance study in hematology care
evidence.venue: Journal of oncology pharmacy practice : official publication of the International Society of Oncology Pharmacy Practitioners
evidence.outcome: Direct detection of intervention-requiring drug-related problems by LLMs versus pharmacist gold standard
evidence.effect: Direct detection limited (51.4%-60.5% across models), nearly half missed initially; guided prompting improved detection to 93.8%-98.1%.
evidence.quote: Direct detection of intervention-requiring DRPs was limited (51.4%-60.5% across models), with nearly half missed initially.

evidence.title: Multimodal Large Language Model for Fracture Detection in Emergency Orthopedic Trauma: A Diagnostic Accuracy Study
evidence.outcome: Missed fractures by LLM, indicating risk of standalone use as diagnosis
evidence.effect: False negatives were 184 patients (16.2% of cohort), 32.4% of LLM-negative assessments; 17.4% of FN cases required surgery; ankle and foot FN rates 30.4% and 17.4%.
evidence.quote: However, its limited ability to detect non-displaced fractures-especially in anatomically complex regions like the ankle and foot-carries direct patient safety implications and confirms that specialist review remains indispensable.

evidence.title: Performance evaluation of 9 large language models in anticoagulation decision-making for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
evidence.venue: Research and practice in thrombosis and haemostasis
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LLMs as stand-alone anticoagulation decision-makers
evidence.effect: Accuracy varied widely and HAS-BLED accuracy was low (8%-51%); authors conclude LLMs remain unsuitable as stand-alone decision-makers.
evidence.quote: At the current stage, LLMs are better suited as auxiliary tools for medical tasks rather than as independent decision-makers.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM responses (100 virtual NVAF patient cases x 9 LLMs)

evidence.title: Diagnosing growth in low-grade gliomas with and without artificial intelligence-measured longitudinal volume measurements: A retrospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Standalone AI growth-call errors
evidence.effect: AI without human review had 25% (4/16) false positives and 8.33% (4/48) false negatives.
evidence.quote: AI without human review generated similar results but with a 25% false positive and an 8.33% false negative rate.

evidence.title: Simulated evaluation of large language model stepwise diagnostic reasoning with real-world chest pain encounters and Bayesian networks
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Suitability of LLM diagnostic output for autonomous use
evidence.effect: Configuration miscalibrated and not suitable for clinical deployment; authors support cautious stance against autonomous diagnostic use and recommend clinician oversight.
evidence.quote: More broadly, our findings suggest that current diagnostic LLMs remain highly sensitive to prompt context and struggle with real-world clinical probabilities, supporting a cautious stance toward autonomous or patient-facing diagnostic use.

evidence.title: Comparative evaluation of multimodal large language models for diagnostic accuracy in pediatric electrocardiography: a prospective comparative diagnostic accuracy study
evidence.outcome: Suitability of multimodal LLM outputs as standalone diagnosis of pediatric ECG
evidence.effect: +LR values near 1.0 across both endpoints; authors conclude standalone deployment is not supported and tools may only serve as adjunctive screening aids under clinician oversight.
evidence.quote: Standalone deployment is not supported; these tools may at most serve as adjunctive screening aids under clinician oversight.

evidence.title: Hidden failure modes of large language models in healthcare-associated infection surveillance: a structured evaluation using NHSN definitions
evidence.outcome: Suitability of LLM output as stand-alone surveillance classification
evidence.effect: Model overcalled HAIs with false positives 33.3% under standard prompt and 7.1% constrained; authors state it cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool, only as decision-support with human final decisions.
evidence.quote: Currently, GPT-5.1 Thinking cannot function as an autonomous HAI surveillance tool.
evidence.sample_unit: case-prompt classifications (70 synthetic vignettes x 3 prompting strategies)

evidence.title: Large language models approach clinician performance in ESC cardiovascular risk stratification: a vignette-based benchmark study
evidence.outcome: Suitability of LLM final risk categorization as stand-alone tool
evidence.effect: Only moderate final classification agreement and major errors in six models; authors conclude LLMs suit supervised augmentation, not autonomous end-to-end risk stratification.
evidence.quote: LLMs may therefore already have practical value as supervised tools for information structuring and eligibility assessment, but not as autonomous end-to-end risk stratification systems.
evidence.sample_unit: simulated clinical vignettes (each in Portuguese and English)

evidence.title: Human versus AI in audiological practice: A comparative evaluation of ChatGPT and physician treatment decisions in idiopathic sudden sensorineural hearing loss
evidence.outcome: Agreement between ChatGPT and physician treatment decisions for ISSNHL (Cohen's Kappa)
evidence.effect: Poor to fair agreement; ChatGPT omitted oral corticosteroids in 26 cases (Kappa 0.029), recommended IV steroids in 20 untreated patients (Kappa 0.393), intratympanic steroids Kappa -0.044, adjunctive therapies Kappa 0.035.
evidence.quote: Overall, poor to fair agreement was observed between AI and clinician treatment decisions.

evidence.title: Pilot Study Comparing Emergency Physician and Artificial Intelligence-supported Interpretations of Electrocardiograms
evidence.venue: The western journal of emergency medicine
evidence.outcome: Reliability of AI ECG interpretation as stand-alone diagnosis/management
evidence.effect: 90% concordance overall, but discrepancies in complex cases and critical management recommendations; authors do not support independent AI use.
evidence.quote: Our findings from this pilot study do not support the independent use of AI for definitive ECG interpretation or emergency management decisions; it should serve as an adjunct tool that enhances rather than supplants human clinical judgment.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models in Infectious Disease Decision-Making: From Examination to Clinical Practice
evidence.outcome: standalone LLM missed serious differential diagnosis
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-R1 and Grok 3 top three differentials omitted invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in Case 1.
evidence.quote: In Case 1 ( Supplementary Table 1 in Supplementary material 2 ), which involved a patient with post-influenza pneumonia and a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, the top three differential diagnoses generated by DeepSeek-R1 and Grok 3 did not include invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

evidence.title: Performance of the Techcyte AI-based image analysis system for coproparasitological diagnosis in clinical stool specimens: a retrospective evaluation study
evidence.outcome: Raw AI standalone false positives
evidence.effect: Before review, 29/31 (93.54%) negative specimens were considered positive due to artifact misclassification.
evidence.quote: Before operator review, most of negative specimens 29/31 (93.54%) were considered positive by the AI-based software due to artifact misclassification.

evidence.title: The Role of AI-Based Software BrainScan in the Interpretation of Non-Contrast Head CT in Acute Ischemic Stroke: An External Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Ischemia detection sensitivity of AI as stand-alone reader
evidence.effect: Ischemia sensitivity 59.2% (95% CI 52.1-66.1), specificity 99.8%, AUC 0.930; lower sensitivity in infratentorial structures; authors recommend rule-in adjunct not stand-alone
evidence.quote: Ischemia sensitivity was 59.2% (95% CI 52.1-66.1) and specificity was 99.8% (99.4-100), with an AUC of 0.930 (0.906-0.954).

evidence.title: Zero-shot detection of apical periodontitis on periapical radiographs using multimodal large language models: diagnostic accuracy and error patterns
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic accuracy of zero-shot MLLMs for apical periodontitis detection, relevant to standalone diagnostic use
evidence.effect: Accuracy up to 71.67% (Gemini). Claude sensitivity 95.00%, specificity 13.33%; GPT-5.2 sensitivity 20.00%, specificity 98.33%. None reliable enough for independent clinical use.
evidence.quote: Although diagnostic performance varied among models, none achieved a level of diagnostic performance sufficient for independent clinical use.

evidence.title: Radiologist-Large Language Model Collaboration in Dermatologic Ultrasound Reporting: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of ChatGPT
evidence.venue: Studies in health technology and informatics
evidence.outcome: stand-alone LLM diagnostic accuracy
evidence.effect: Condition 2, LLM reporting based solely on image, had 26.2% diagnostic accuracy versus radiologist 55.4%.
evidence.quote: Diagnostic accuracy was highest in Condition 3 (83.2%), compared with Condition 1 (55.4%) and Condition 2 (26.2%) (p<0.001).

evidence.title: Performance of DeepSeek V3.2 and ChatGPT 5.1 in Musculoskeletal Triage and Differential Diagnosis of Outpatients With Low Back Pain: Multidimensional Comparative Study
evidence.outcome: Triage and preliminary diagnosis accuracy of LLMs as potential stand-alone tools
evidence.effect: Suboptimal red-flag sensitivity; preliminary diagnosis accuracy 76.7% (DeepSeek) and 87.5% (ChatGPT) with structured input; authors state models should not be used stand-alone without clinician oversight.
evidence.quote: However, their suboptimal sensitivity for red-flag conditions such as MM highlights significant safety concerns, indicating that they should not be used as stand-alone triage tools without clinician oversight.

evidence.title: Diagnostic accuracy of ChatGPT-5 in evaluating root canal treatment and periapical pathosis on periapical radiographs
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of ChatGPT-5 for detecting obturation errors, voids, and periapical lesions on radiographs
evidence.effect: Low sensitivity for short (13.7%) or long (0.0%) obturations, voids (9.0%-22.7%), and periapical lesions (10.5%-28.6%); high specificity up to 99.3%.
evidence.quote: ChatGPT-5 demonstrated high specificity (up to 99.3%) for normal or adequately treated findings but low sensitivity for short (13.7%) or long (0.0%) obturations, voids (9.0%-22.7%), and periapical lesions (10.5%-28.6%).

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence meets pediatric orthopedics: A comparative analysis of ChatGPT-4o, Gemini 2.0, and Claude 3.5 in detecting supracondylar humeral fractures
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of LLMs as standalone diagnostic tools for supracondylar fractures
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 68.4% (Gemini 2.0), 58.7% (Claude 3.5), and 19.3% (ChatGPT-4o); specificity was low (33.1-36.0%), giving many missed fractures and false positives.
evidence.quote: Current LLMs demonstrate limited capability as independent diagnostic tools for pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures.

evidence.title: Potential and Pitfalls of Multimodal Large Language Models in Cerebral Palsy Hip Surveillance: A Radiographic Interpretation Study Assessing Educational Utility
evidence.outcome: Whether MLLM diagnostic accuracy supports use as stand-alone diagnostic tool
evidence.effect: Significant radiographic hallucinations and lack of specific evidence-based guidance preclude standalone diagnostic use; MLLMs suggested as educational adjuncts requiring expert oversight.
evidence.quote: However, significant radiographic hallucinations and a lack of specific, evidence-based guidance preclude their use as standalone diagnostic tools.
evidence.sample_unit: deidentified pediatric pelvic radiographs (with 9 caregiver prompts each; ~95 responses per model)

evidence.title: Prompt Configurations for Multimodal Large Language Models in Diagnosing and Staging Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head: Multimodel Retrospective Observational Diagnostic Study
evidence.outcome: Stand-alone diagnostic performance of MLLMs for ONFH detection and grading
evidence.effect: Single-image detection AUC 0.50-0.58 (mean 0.55); detailed ARCO grading accuracy 0.22 with SI; authors conclude none should be used independently for clinical decision-making.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, none of the evaluated models should currently be used independently for clinical decision-making.

evidence.title: The Role of Google Gemini in the Interpretation of Ovarian Lesions
evidence.outcome: Risk of missed or incorrect diagnoses if the AI output were used as stand-alone diagnosis
evidence.effect: Gemini misclassified 3/10 malignant cases as benign (O-RADS 2, GQS 1) and overdiagnosed 6/10 normal ovaries as pathologic; authors conclude it is not ready for independent clinical application.
evidence.quote: Google Gemini seems to not be ready for independent clinical application in ovarian ultrasound interpretation.

evidence.title: Large language model accuracy in inhaler technique counselling for asthma and COPD: A comparison of free and paid models across ten devices
evidence.outcome: Safety-warning omissions and variability in LLM inhaler instructions, arguing against stand-alone use
evidence.effect: Safety-warning coverage was 62.4% in free and 75.3% in paid tiers; critical errors 0.48 free vs 0.02 paid; authors argue against autonomous LLM use.
evidence.quote: Safety-warning omissions and test-retest variability argue against autonomous LLM use; these tools are best deployed as adjuncts to clinician- and pharmacist-led teach-back education.

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Model-Generated Recommendations in Glaucoma Surgical Decision-Making
evidence.outcome: LLM surgical recommendation quality and safety risk by case complexity
evidence.effect: Gemini appropriateness and rationale quality dropped significantly in complex cases with increased safety risk (p = .009); ChatGPT and Copilot rationale quality lower in complex cases (p = .014, <0.001).
evidence.quote: For Gemini, appropriateness and rationale quality scores dropped significantly in complex cases and were accompanied by a statistically significant increase in safety risk (p = .009).

evidence.title: Concordance between GPT-4 and a multidisciplinary tumor board in pancreatic cancer: A prospective pilot study
evidence.outcome: GPT-4 recommending inappropriate management in complex cases, showing unsuitability as stand-alone decision-maker
evidence.effect: 12 of 45 recommendations discordant with MDT; in one case GPT-4 advised resection despite CT report stating resectability could not be determined.
evidence.quote: While these observations remain correlative, they are consistent with the notion that LLMs, in their current form, are not capable of serving as stand-alone decision-makers and that expert judgment remains a critical factor [ 25 ].

evidence.title: Diagnostic Performance and Confidence Calibration of Large Language Models for Bone Tumor Radiographs
evidence.outcome: False negative and false positive rates of LLM radiograph interpretation
evidence.effect: False negative rates: GPT-4.1 29.9%, ChatGPT 24.8%, Gemini 6.6%. False positive abnormality rates: GPT-4.1 40.7%, Gemini 25.9%, ChatGPT 13.5%.
evidence.quote: False negative rates varied substantially, with GPT-4.1 demonstrating the highest rate (29.9%), followed by ChatGPT (24.8%) and Gemini (6.6%).

evidence.title: AICyte-alone capabilities as an independent screener for triaging cervical cytology using a 50% negative cutoff value
evidence.outcome: AI-alone false-negative cytology
evidence.effect: 49 LSIL-or-higher cases were designated no further review; cytohistologic correlation found eight CIN1 and 18 negative, with remaining cases without histologic follow-up.
evidence.quote: Of the 49 low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion or higher that were designed by AICyte as not needing further review, the cytohistologic correlation revealed eight cases of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia 1 and 18 negative cases; and the remaining cases were without histologic follow-up.

evidence.title: A Multimodal Large Language Model as an End-to-End Classifier of Thyroid Nodule Malignancy Risk: Usability Study
evidence.outcome: stand-alone TI-RADS classification accuracy
evidence.effect: Even the best overall TI-RADS classification accuracy was only 57.3%.
evidence.quote: The best accuracy obtained for overall TI-RADS classification level was still only 57.3%.

evidence.title: ChatGPT in Oral Pathology: Bright Promise or Diagnostic Mirage
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic sensitivity of ChatGPT-4o for OSCC, oral leukoplakia and oral lichen planus from clinical photographs
evidence.effect: Sensitivity was 65% for OSCC, 60% for OL and 25% for OLP; specificity 96.1-100%; a significant proportion of true cases were missed, so it cannot serve as a standalone diagnostic tool.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, its sensitivity remains insufficient, as a significant proportion of true cases were missed, underscoring that the model cannot be relied upon as a standalone diagnostic tool.

evidence.title: Automated Tumor and Node Staging from Esophageal Cancer Endoscopic Ultrasound Reports: A Benchmark of Advanced Reasoning Models with Prompt Engineering and Cross-Lingual Evaluation
evidence.outcome: Clinically consequential cross-stage misclassification errors in N-staging
evidence.effect: Grok-3 misclassified 30.3% of N3 cases as N1; Qwen3 classified 91.8% of N0, 89.8% of N1 and 92.7% of N3 as N2 in English without-prompt; DeepSeek-R1 errors mostly adjacent.
evidence.quote: Grok-3, for example, misclassified 30.3% of N3 cases as the distant N1 stage under identical conditions ( Supplementary Material , Figures S1–S4 ).
evidence.sample_unit: endoscopic ultrasound reports (625 for T-staging, 579 for N-staging)

evidence.title: Benchmark evaluation of large language models for clinical decision support in headache management
evidence.venue: Journal of oral & facial pain and headache
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM diagnostic performance suffices for standalone use versus adjunct decision support
evidence.effect: Overall clinical accuracy remained below expert performance and insufficient for unsupervised clinical use; LLMs should serve as decision support rather than stand-alone diagnostic tools.
evidence.quote: These findings emphasize that LLMs should be used as decision support tools rather than stand-alone diagnostic tools, especially in high-risk situations.

evidence.title: Real-world performance of open-source large language models in diabetes diagnosis
evidence.outcome: LLM hallucination and reasoning errors in rule-based diagnosis
evidence.effect: In 0.83% of cases with absent indicators the model still generated a positive DKD diagnosis; 49.77% of MetS cases self-identified as meeting ≥3 criteria were misclassified.
evidence.quote: Furthermore, even when at least one indicator was successfully extracted, the diagnostic error rate remained at 27.02%.

evidence.title: From ABCD to AI: Assessing the Diagnostic Reliability of MLLMs in Cutaneous Melanoma Screening-A Head-to-Head Comparison
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of MLLMs for melanoma screening when used as standalone tools
evidence.effect: All models missed about half of malignant lesions; Grok 4 sensitivity 52%; Gemini 3 accuracy 71%, specificity 94%.
evidence.quote: All models exhibited a critical deficit in sensitivity, missing approximately half of the malignant lesions.

evidence.title: A Generalizable and Interpretable Framework for Molecular Subtype Classification of Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Integrating Conformal Uncertainty Quantification and Consensus-Based Explainable Artificial Intelligence Across Multiple Cohorts
evidence.outcome: Suitability for autonomous use versus decision-support given conformal undercoverage
evidence.effect: Even best procedure (CRC) reached only 85.3% coverage vs 95% target; authors do not recommend autonomous use and confine tool to decision support under expert oversight.
evidence.quote: However, because even CRC attains only 85.3% empirical coverage against the 0.95 target, we explicitly do not recommend any of these procedures for autonomous clinical use at α = 0.05.
evidence.sample_unit: tumor samples (140 CPTAC discovery, 150 TCGA external)
evidence.country: Not reported (public US cohorts CPTAC-PDAC and TCGA-PAAD; authors' future work references Turkey)

commentary.bottom_line: Across 31 studies, clinician review of AI output generally reduced false positives compared with AI operating alone, though some studies found no difference or a loss of sensitivity after human review. No randomized trial has tested the practice, and the outcomes measured were diagnostic accuracy rather than patient harm, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: Seven of the 31 studies were prospective or quasi-experimental in real deployments, and none was randomized. Most compared clinician-plus-AI with AI alone on accuracy rather than on patient outcomes. Results mostly favored adjunct use, but two real-deployment studies found no significant difference and one found lower sensitivity after human review, so certainty is low.

In a real deployment for intracranial hemorrhage, AI alone produced 293 false positives versus 4 for radiologists with AI. In a fracture replay, AI used as a safety net had 0.07% false negatives versus 1.5% standalone, with false positives of 7.6% versus 6.8%. In a screening replay, standalone AI had lower sensitivity than standard care (75.0% vs 79.8%).

Human review can also introduce errors. In a teledermatology deployment, review raised specificity from 76.8% to 86.8% but lowered sensitivity from 82.5% to 75.3%. Among emergency interns, blended use cut missed diagnoses (6.7% vs 14.3%) but raised misdiagnosis (6.2% vs 3.3%). In Norway, radiographer supervision changed the patient pathway in 20% of cases compared with AI alone.

Four tests reported populations of interest. These included rural patients in Ukraine and China, a blood gas replay in Mexico involving a limited English or non-English population, and a US emergency department study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients. None enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The Mexico study was an offline replay conducted outside US care.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that a device should not replace standard-of-care diagnosis and should be applied jointly with clinician judgment. The recommendation aligns with that labeling expectation. No test of the practice examined whether deployments followed labeled intended use, so the evidence cannot show whether labeling adherence itself reduces diagnostic error.

In a screening deployment among women in Spain, AI-supported reading raised cancer detection from 5.8\u2030 to 9.0	o 9.0\u2030 and recall from 5.4% to 6.1%, with radiologists making the final recall decision. Two offline replays reported workload reductions of 76.7% and 85.5% when AI triaged cases for selective clinician review, but these configurations were not tested in live workflows.

commentary.research_gap: No randomized or cluster-randomized trial has compared adjunct use with standalone AI or with usual care on patient outcomes such as missed diagnoses, delayed treatment, or harm. Future studies should measure when human review adds errors, as seen in the loss of sensitivity after teledermatology review. They should also measure reviewer workload and include safety-net and limited English proficiency settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and none addressed limited English proficiency in US care. Rural cohorts in Ukraine and China, an offline replay in Mexico involving a limited English or non-English population, and one US emergency department study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients offer partial coverage. The effect of requiring clinician review in under-resourced settings, where qualified reviewers may be scarce, remains untested.
